## Why venting is non-negotiable

A compressor AC doesn't "make cold" — it moves heat. Everything it pulls out of the room air, plus the electrical waste heat of the compressor itself, leaves through the exhaust hose. Run the unit with the hose lying in the room and you have a very expensive fan heater with extra steps: guides that have measured or documented this consistently conclude an unvented portable AC leaves the room the same temperature or slightly warmer (see for example the venting overview at LearnMetrics).

## The 5 real routes, compared

Route | Renter-safe? | Effort | Catch |

Door seal kit (hallway, stairwell or adjoining room) | ✅ Yes | 15–30 min | The adjoining space absorbs the heat — fine for a stairwell, bad for the bedroom next door |

Balcony / French door, tilted + seal | ✅ Yes | 15–30 min | Same technique as a tilt window; needs a door that opens |

Through-wall vent (core-drilled, outside grille) | ❌ Permission needed | Trade job | Permanent hole; but the best airflow of all routes |

Utility room / drop ceiling | ⚠️ Depends | 30–60 min | Heat has to go somewhere — only works if that space is big, unused and ideally ventilated |

Chimney flue (unused) | ❌ Professional only | Trade job | Must be checked and approved by a chimney sweep first — never improvise this |

## Route 1: the door seal kit (start here)

This is the same fabric-and-zip principle as the window kits our tilt-and-turn window guide recommends — just cut for a door frame. You tape or velcro the fabric around the frame, zip the hose through, and the door can still be opened in an emergency.

- Pick the right door. Best: a door to a stairwell, hallway or large unused room. Worst: the door to the room where someone sleeps — you'd be heating it.

- Measure first. Kits are sized for standard door frames (roughly 210 cm height); measure your frame and the hose diameter before ordering.

- Seal honestly. Gaps let the hot air circle straight back — the seal, not the hose, decides how well the room cools.

Door seal kits for portable ACs
Fabric kits with zips, sized for door frames — search current offers by name:

Check door seal kits on Amazon →

## Route 2: a balcony or French door, tilted

If the room has a balcony door but no usable window, treat the door exactly like an oversized tilt window: tilt it, seal the wedge-shaped opening with a fabric kit, and run the hose through the sealed gap. The step-by-step is identical to the tilt-window method — including the mistake of running the unit with the door simply "open a crack", which feeds the exhaust heat straight back inside.

## Route 3: the through-wall vent — best airflow, biggest commitment

A core-drilled hole (usually 130–160 mm) with an outside grille and a back-draught flap gives the cleanest, shortest exhaust path and finally frees the window entirely. But it is a permanent alteration: in a rented flat you need written landlord permission, and in an owned flat the exterior wall may count as communal property that requires the owners' association to agree. If you're allowed, it's the one route that turns a portable AC into a semi-fixed installation — and it pairs well with hose insulation, as covered in our hose extension guide.

## Routes 4 & 5: utility rooms, ceilings, chimneys — the conditional ones

Utility room / drop ceiling: venting into another indoor space only relocates the heat. That's acceptable if the space is large, unused and ideally has its own ventilation (a storage room with an outside grille, a garage) — and pointless if it's a small closed cupboard, which will heat up until the heat leaks right back.

Chimney flue: an unused flue can technically carry exhaust air, but flues can be shared, blocked, or still serve other flats. In Germany and most of Europe the chimney sweep (Schornsteinfeger) must approve any such use. Never route exhaust into a flue on your own judgement.

The route that usually fails: dryer ducts. Typical portable AC hoses are 125–150 mm across; most dryer wall ducts are narrower. Forcing the exhaust through a smaller duct raises back-pressure, so the unit cools worse, runs longer and can overheat. Only consider it if the duct diameter genuinely matches the hose.

## If there is truly no route: stop fighting the physics

A room with no window, no suitable door, no wall you may drill and no approved flue cannot host a compressor AC — and no accessory changes that. The honest alternatives: an evaporative air cooler (no exhaust needed, works best in dry heat, adds humidity), aggressive shading and night-time cross-ventilation, and cooling the person rather than the room. Our German guide to cooling windowless rooms ranks these fallbacks in detail.

## Frequently asked questions

Can I run a portable air conditioner without venting it at all?You can switch it on, but it will not cool the room. A portable AC moves heat from the room air into its exhaust; if that exhaust stays in the room, all the heat — plus the waste heat of the compressor — is released right back, so the room ends up slightly warmer than before.

What is the best venting option in a rented flat with no usable window?A door seal kit on a door that leads to a hallway, stairwell or another room you don't need cool. It is fabric, attaches with zips or hook-and-loop tape, leaves no damage and needs no landlord permission — the same principle as the window kits, just cut for a door frame.

Can I vent a portable AC into a dryer vent?Usually not in Europe. Most portable AC exhaust hoses are around 125–150 mm in diameter, while typical dryer wall ducts are narrower, and squeezing the airflow raises back-pressure so the unit cools worse and can overheat. Treat it as a last resort only if the duct diameter genuinely matches.

What if there is truly no venting route at all?Then a compressor AC is the wrong tool. An evaporative air cooler needs no exhaust hose and helps in dry heat, though it adds humidity and cools far less. Combined with shading and night ventilation it is the honest fallback for a room with no venting route.

## Window Seal for Portable ACs: Which Type Fits? (2026)
URL: https://getecoback.com/en/guide/window-seal-portable-ac.html

Fits most windowsWindow seal kit (hook-and-loop)→For skylightsRoof-window seal→For the leftover gapsFoam sealing tape→All models with reasoning ↓

🗓 Updated August 8, 2026 · EcoBack editorial team

The window seal is the most-bought accessory around portable air conditioners — and the one where most purchases go wrong: the wrong type for the window, a length that is too short, tape that lets go in the sun. Here is the decision in three steps: type, length, mounting.

Short answer: For a tilt or tilt-and-turn window, take the universal velcro fabric seal (from ~€15–25, HOOMEE-style) — or a rigid outlet panel if the unit runs at the same window all summer. For a roof window you need the dedicated roof-window version. Length = 2 × (sash width + sash height), next size up when in doubt. And degrease the frame first — it is almost always the tape that fails, not the fabric.

## Why (almost) nothing cools without a seal

A portable AC blows several hundred cubic metres of warm room air out through the hose every hour. That air is missing from the room — negative pressure builds, and it pulls outside air in through every opening. If the window is simply tilted open, the 35-degree air comes straight back: the unit cools against itself, runs non-stop and still manages only two or three degrees. That is why the seal is not an "accessory" but half the cooling capacity — the most effective single purchase in the whole setup.

## The three types — and who each one is for

Universal classic
Velcro fabric seal (HOOMEE-style, many near-identical brands) — a fabric sleeve with a zip that wraps the whole tilted sash, attached with velcro strips. Fits tilt, tilt-and-turn and most casement windows, comes off without residue when you move out — which makes it the default for renters.

✓ Cheap (approx. €15–25)   ✓ fits almost everywhere   ✓ renter-friendly   ✕ Window stays tilted = not lockable   ✕ the tape is the weak point

See velcro seals →

For all-summer use
Rigid outlet panel (Eurom "Window Way Out"-style, or a cut-to-size hollow-chamber sheet) — a solid panel with a hose port that clamps into the tilt opening. Seals noticeably better than fabric, the window is nearly closed, and the hose gets a fixed connection.

✓ Best sealing   ✓ nothing flaps   ✓ clamps instead of glues   ✕ Pricier (from ~€40–60)   ✕ must match your window size

See outlet panels →

For roof windows
Roof-window seal — the same fabric idea, but cut for pivot and top-hung roof windows (Velux & co.). Important here: the opening must point downward and rain must not run in along the hose — details in the roof-window guide.

✓ The only clean solution on a roof window   ✕ Watch out in rain   ✕ fitting is a little fiddlier

See roof-window versions →

## What length do you need?

The most common mispurchase is a seal that is too short. The rule: measure the moving sash (not the frame), and the seal must wrap its full perimeter — so 2 × (width + height). A typical 60 × 140 cm window therefore needs 4 m. Common off-the-shelf lengths are ~300, 400 and 560 cm; when in doubt take the next size up — extra length can be gathered, a gap cannot. The calculator at the top of this page does the maths for you and names the size that fits.

## Glue or clamp? The honest weak point

In buyer reviews, fabric seals almost never fail at the fabric — they fail at the supplied adhesive tape. A white window frame in direct sun reaches 50–60 °C; the glue underneath softens, the tape lets go and leaves residue when peeled off. Three countermeasures:

- Degrease before sticking: wipe the frame with washing-up liquid, dry it, press the tape on firmly and let it rest unloaded for 24 h — this practically doubles the hold, for free.

- Clamp instead of glue where you can: outlet panels and some fabric variants clamp into the tilt opening — no glue, no residue, no mid-summer failure.

- Do not reach for heavy-duty universal tape: stronger third-party tape holds, but wrecks paint or the rubber gasket on removal — an expensive swap when you move out.

## Frequently asked questions

Which window seal is best for tilt windows?For occasional use, the universal velcro fabric seal (from around €15–25): it wraps the whole tilted sash and comes off without residue — which is why it is the default for renters. If the unit runs at the same window all summer, a rigid outlet panel seals better and keeps the window nearly closed, but costs more and has to match your window size.

What length does the window seal need to be?Measure the moving sash (not the frame) and calculate 2 × (width + height) — that is the perimeter the seal has to wrap. A typical 60 × 140 cm window needs 4 metres. Common off-the-shelf lengths are around 300, 400 and 560 cm; when in doubt take the next size up — extra length can be gathered, a gap cannot.

Why does the window seal keep coming off?The weak point is almost never the fabric but the supplied adhesive tape: in direct sun the frame reaches 50 to 60 degrees Celsius, the glue softens, lets go and leaves residue. Degrease the frame with washing-up liquid before sticking, press firmly and let it rest for 24 hours — or choose a variant that clamps instead of glues.

Does a window seal actually make a difference?Yes — it is the most effective single purchase in the whole setup. A portable AC pushes room air outside and creates negative pressure: without a seal, hot outside air streams straight back in through the open window and the unit cools against itself. With a tight seal the same unit reaches the target temperature faster and cycles less afterwards.
